title: Hours, Not Seconds, Not Days
subtitle: A man whose left ear keeps failing, from the third attack to the first prescription
description: Sorting vertigo by how long it lasts, reading a low-frequency audiogram, finding the fluctuation in the old chart, closing the mimics by asking, scanning for the one you cannot ask away, counting the criteria, and first-line management and what not to give daily.

steps.title: Step 1/7: How Long It Lasts
steps.scenario:
A 62-year-old man, brought by his wife.

    Complaint       attacks of the room spinning
    Each attack     2 to 4 hours, with vomiting
    Afterward       a day of unsteadiness, then normal
    Frequency       2 or 3 a month, for a year
    Today           no attack

Left ear
    Tinnitus        roaring, most of the time
    Fullness        builds just before an attack
    Hearing         drops during attacks, partly comes back

Right ear         fine
Headache          none with attacks; no light or sound sensitivity

Past
    Admitted twice     for "sudden hearing loss", left, each time with vertigo; steroids given
    Emergency CT       brain, after one attack: normal
steps.question: What does the time course tell you?

options.text: (A) Attacks lasting seconds with head position: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
(B) One attack lasting days: vestibular neuritis
(C) Recurrent attacks lasting hours, with hearing, tinnitus and fullness in one ear that change around the attacks: the pattern of Meniere's disease, which needs a documented hearing loss to confirm
(D) Attacks of any length with headache: vestibular migraine

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Duration sorts vertigo before anything else does.
• Seconds, brought on by turning over or looking up: BPPV.
• Minutes to hours, recurrent, with a normal ear between attacks and often a headache: vestibular migraine.
• Hours, recurrent, with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness in one ear that fluctuate with the attacks: Meniere's disease.
• Days, a single continuous episode, hearing normal: vestibular neuritis.

His attacks last hours and come back, and his left ear tells the rest of the story: a roaring tinnitus, fullness that builds before an attack, hearing that drops and partly recovers. That is endolymphatic hydrops behaving as it does, and it is the clinical picture of Meniere's disease. What it is not yet is a diagnosis, because the criteria require the hearing loss to be documented on an audiogram, not just described.

The two admissions for sudden hearing loss are worth a second look. Sudden sensorineural loss with vertigo and roaring tinnitus that partly recovers, and then happens again in the same ear, is how Meniere's disease often first presents. Each admission treated an attack; nobody yet connected the attacks.

Why the others fail:
(A) BPPV lasts seconds to a minute and is positional. Hours of spinning with vomiting is not a canal problem.
(B) Vestibular neuritis is one attack lasting days, and it does not come back three times a month. His are recurrent and shorter.
(D) Vestibular migraine is the main alternative and must be asked about, but he has no headache, no photophobia or phonophobia with attacks, and migraine does not produce a fluctuating hearing loss in one ear.

Keypoint: hours, recurrent, one ear with fluctuating hearing, tinnitus and fullness: suspect Meniere's disease, and the next step is the audiogram that will confirm or refute it.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55. doi:10.1177/0194599820909438.

steps.title: Step 2/7: Today's Audiogram
steps.scenario:
Otoscopy          both drums normal
Weber             to the right
Rinne             normal, both sides

Audiogram today, between attacks:

    Left     250 Hz 55 / 500 Hz 50 / 1 kHz 45 / 2 kHz 30 / 4 kHz 25 / 8 kHz 25 dB HL
    Right    10 to 20 dB HL across
    Speech discrimination, left    72 percent
steps.media: Load image: Pure-tone audiogram from this patient, de-identified, unannotated. Caption: 'Audiogram, between attacks.'
steps.question: What is the pattern, and why does it matter?

options.text: (A) A rising, low-frequency sensorineural loss on the left, worst at 250 to 1000 Hz: the audiometric signature of endolymphatic hydrops, and the criterion that names the affected ear
(B) A high-frequency loss on the left: noise damage from his work
(C) A flat loss on the left: the residue of his two sudden hearing losses, unrelated to the vertigo
(D) A conductive loss on the left, from fluid behind the drum

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Most sensorineural losses slope downward: high frequencies go first, in age, in noise, in most ototoxicity. Meniere's disease does the opposite. The hydrops distorts the cochlear apex first, where the low frequencies are coded, so the early audiogram rises: worst at 250 to 1000 Hz, better toward 4000 and 8000. As the disease goes on the loss flattens and spreads, but in the first years the rising shape is the clue.

The Barany criteria make this the deciding criterion. Definite Meniere's disease requires a low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss in one ear, documented on audiometry on at least one occasion, before, during or after an attack. His left ear, 55 dB at 250 Hz rising to 25 dB at 4 kHz, with a normal right ear, is that. This audiogram does two things: it meets the criterion, and it names the ear.

The tuning forks agree: Weber to the right, the better cochlea, and Rinne normal on both sides. Sensorineural, left.

Why the others fail:
(B) Noise and age damage the high frequencies first. His high frequencies are the best part of his left ear. This is the reverse of a noise notch.
(C) The loss is not flat; it rises. Whether the two sudden losses were unrelated is the next step's question, and the shape of this curve already suggests the answer.
(D) Rinne is normal, the drum is normal, and Weber went to the other ear. Nothing here is conductive.

Keypoint: a rising, low-frequency sensorineural loss in one ear with episodic vertigo meets the hearing criterion and names the ear.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statement 3.

steps.title: Step 3/7: The Old Chart
steps.scenario:
Before he leaves, you pull the record from his last admission for "sudden hearing loss".
That audiogram was done on the day of the attack.

During the attack, left
    250 Hz 70 / 500 Hz 65 / 1 kHz 55 / 2 kHz 35 / 4 kHz 25 / 8 kHz 25 dB HL

Today, between attacks, left
    250 Hz 55 / 500 Hz 50 / 1 kHz 45 / 2 kHz 30 / 4 kHz 25 / 8 kHz 25 dB HL

Right ear    10 to 20 dB HL across, both times
steps.media: Load image: The two audiograms from this patient side by side, from the admission on the day of an attack and today between attacks, de-identified, unannotated. Caption: 'Audiograms, during and between attacks.'
steps.question: What does the old audiogram add?

options.text: (A) It shows the hearing has progressed to a fixed loss since the admission
(B) It shows a separate sudden sensorineural loss that recovered, unrelated to today's picture
(C) It shows the right ear was also involved at the time

(D) It shows the loss fluctuates: 10 to 15 dB worse in the low frequencies during an attack, identical in the highs, partly recovered between; and it shows the "sudden hearing loss" was an attack of the same disease

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Lay the two curves over each other. During the attack the low frequencies were 70, 65 and 55 dB; between attacks they are 55, 50 and 45. The high frequencies are 25 on both days. That is fluctuation: the loss swings at the apex with each attack and partly recovers, and it leaves the base alone. One audiogram names the ear and meets the criterion. Two audiograms show the disease doing what it does, and they show it on paper, which is stronger than his account of hearing that "drops and partly comes back".

The old chart also closes a loop. The audiogram that was filed as a sudden sensorineural hearing loss is the same rising, low-frequency curve, taken at the top of the swing. Sudden hearing loss with vertigo and roaring tinnitus that partly recovers, and then happens again in the same ear, is how Meniere's disease often first presents. Each admission treated an attack; nobody connected them. The diagnosis was in his chart years ago.

From here, repeat the audiogram at follow-up visits. Serial tests do three things: they document how far the low frequencies swing, they show when they stop swinging and settle into a fixed loss as the disease matures, and they watch the other ear, which becomes involved in a minority of patients over the years.

Why the others fail:
(A) The opposite. The loss is better today than during the admission, and the difference is confined to the low frequencies. That is recovery between attacks, not progression.
(B) A sudden sensorineural loss that recovered would have been flat or downsloping and would not have come back in the same ear with the same rising shape. Same ear, same curve, same attacks: one disease.
(C) The right ear was 10 to 20 dB across on both occasions. Unilateral.

Keypoint: two audiograms, one during and one between attacks, show the low frequencies swinging and the highs standing still; the fluctuation is documented, and the old admissions were the first attacks.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statement 3.

steps.title: Step 4/7: What Else Looks Like This
steps.scenario:
Recurrent vertigo lasting hours.
One ear: fluctuating low-frequency loss, tinnitus, fullness.

Before naming anything, you go through what else can look like this.

    Headache          none with attacks; no photophobia or phonophobia; no migraine history
    Loud sound        does not provoke vertigo
    Straining         does not provoke vertigo; no autophony
    Neurology         no diplopia, dysarthria, weakness or ataxia; gait normal between attacks
    Other ear         normal; no rapid bilateral change
    Systemic          no rash, joint or eye disease; no barotrauma or head injury
steps.question: Which conditions must you consider, and what would it take to address each?

options.text: (A) Only a vestibular schwannoma; an MRI settles the whole differential

(B) Vestibular migraine, by history and the migraine criteria; superior canal dehiscence, by temporal bone CT and VEMPs if sound- or pressure-induced symptoms or an air-bone gap appear; a lesion on the nerve, by MRI of the internal auditory canals; a central cause, by neurological examination and the same MRI; autoimmune disease, by serology if the loss turns rapid or bilateral
(C) None; the picture is clear enough to diagnose without considering alternatives
(D) Calorics and electrocochleography first; they will tell the conditions apart

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

Episodic vertigo with one-sided aural symptoms has a short list of look-alikes. The history lowers the suspicion for most of them; it does not, on its own, prove any of them absent. What it does is tell you which tests are worth doing and which are not.

Vestibular migraine. The most important mimic: recurrent spontaneous vertigo lasting minutes to hours, sometimes with aural symptoms. There is no test for it. It is addressed by the history against the migraine criteria, and by the audiogram: migraine does not produce a fluctuating low-frequency loss in one ear. His answers make it unlikely, and the two audiograms make it unlikelier. It stays on the list until the pattern has declared itself over follow-up.

Superior semicircular canal dehiscence. Vertigo set off by loud sound or by straining, autophony, and a low-frequency air-bone gap. His answers and his normal Rinne make it unlikely, so the confirmatory tests, a temporal bone CT and cervical VEMPs with lowered thresholds, are not ordered today. They are ordered the moment those features appear.

A lesion on the nerve. A vestibular schwannoma presents with an asymmetric sensorineural loss, tinnitus, and sometimes episodic vertigo, and it can wear this exact picture for years. Nothing in the history addresses it. It is addressed by MRI of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium, and the guideline says to offer that scan to anyone with an asymmetric sensorineural loss. That is the next step.

A central cause. A stroke or a posterior fossa lesion usually declares itself with neurological signs, and his examination is normal. The same MRI that looks at the canals looks at the posterior fossa.

Autoimmune inner ear disease. A rapidly progressive, usually bilateral loss, often with systemic disease. His is slow and one-sided. It would be addressed by serology and a trial of steroids if the other ear started to move.

Why the others fail:
(A) The MRI addresses the nerve and the posterior fossa. It says nothing about migraine or dehiscence, which are addressed by history, criteria, and, if suspected, a different scan.
(C) The fourth diagnostic criterion is that nothing else explains the picture better. Skipping the differential is skipping the criterion.
(D) Calorics measure how much the ear has lost and electrocochleography looks for hydrops indirectly. Neither separates these conditions, and the guideline says not to use them to make the diagnosis.

Keypoint: migraine is addressed by criteria and the audiogram, dehiscence by CT and VEMPs only if the symptoms appear, the nerve and the posterior fossa by one MRI; the history tells you which tests to order, not which diagnoses to skip.

Reference: Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 2, 4 and 5. Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7.

steps.title: Step 5/7: The Scan
steps.scenario:
One alternative that history cannot address:
a lesion on the nerve, behind an asymmetric sensorineural loss.

He mentions the emergency brain CT was normal.
He asks whether that settles it.
steps.media: Load image: Axial T1 post-contrast MRI through the internal auditory canals from this patient, de-identified, unannotated. Caption: 'MRI, internal auditory canals.'
steps.question: Which investigation do you order, and which do you not?

options.text: (A) Caloric testing and electrocochleography, to confirm the hydrops objectively
(B) Nothing; the normal CT already excluded a tumor
(C) CT of the temporal bones with contrast
(D) MRI of the internal auditory canals and posterior fossa with gadolinium, to exclude a vestibular schwannoma behind an asymmetric sensorineural loss; no routine vestibular testing, no repeat CT

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Vestibular schwannoma. It presents with an asymmetric sensorineural loss, tinnitus, and sometimes episodic vertigo, and it can mimic episodic inner-ear disease for years. The guideline says to offer MRI of the internal auditory canals and posterior fossa with gadolinium to any patient with an asymmetric sensorineural loss, and he has one. The scan is not done to confirm a diagnosis; it is done to remove the alternative that would change everything. His was normal, which is what most are, and with that the last mimic is closed.

What not to order routinely:
• Vestibular function tests. Calorics, video head impulse and VEMPs measure how much the left ear has lost. Useful later, when weighing an ablative treatment; not how a diagnosis is made.
• Electrocochleography. Inconsistent, and the guideline says not to use it to establish a diagnosis.
• Another CT. It does not show the nerve or the labyrinth's contents. The emergency CT answered a different question.

Why the others fail:
(A) Neither test is part of the diagnostic criteria, and the guideline recommends against ordering them routinely to make the diagnosis. They do not exclude a tumor.
(B) A normal brain CT does not exclude a schwannoma in the internal auditory canal. Small ones are invisible on CT.
(C) Temporal bone CT is the test for a dehiscence, which his history has already excluded. The lesion still open is soft tissue in the canal, and MRI is the test for that.

Keypoint: asymmetric sensorineural loss gets an MRI of the internal auditory canals; a normal CT excludes nothing on the nerve.

Reference: Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 4, 5 and 6.

steps.title: Step 6/7: Definite or Probable
steps.scenario:
What you have:

    Vertigo           recurrent, spontaneous, 2 to 4 hours each, many in a year
    Hearing           low-frequency sensorineural loss, left, on two audiograms; worse during an attack
    Aural symptoms    left tinnitus, fullness and hearing fluctuate with attacks
    Alternatives      mimics addressed on history; MRI of the internal auditory canals normal

The Barany Society criteria are shown.
steps.media: Load image: Your own table of the Barany Society 2015 criteria, redrawn: Definite = two or more spontaneous vertigo episodes of 20 minutes to 12 hours; audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency sensorineural loss in one ear on at least one occasion before, during or after an episode; fluctuating aural symptoms in that ear; not better explained. Probable = two or more episodes of 20 minutes to 24 hours; fluctuating aural symptoms; not better explained. No row highlighted. Caption: 'Barany Society criteria, 2015.'
steps.question: Using the criteria shown, what is the diagnosis?

options.text: (A) Definite Meniere's disease: two or more attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours, audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency loss in the affected ear, fluctuating aural symptoms in that ear, and no better explanation
(B) Probable Meniere's disease, because the hearing loss was documented between attacks rather than during one
(C) Probable Meniere's disease, because the criteria require imaging evidence of hydrops
(D) Meniere's disease cannot be diagnosed without electrocochleography

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The Barany Society criteria have two tiers, and the difference is the audiogram.

Definite Meniere's disease, all four:
1. Two or more spontaneous episodes of vertigo, each lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours.
2. Audiometrically documented low- to mid-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in one ear, defining the affected ear, on at least one occasion before, during or after an episode.
3. Fluctuating aural symptoms in the affected ear: hearing, tinnitus or fullness.
4. Not better accounted for by another vestibular diagnosis.

Probable Meniere's disease: two or more episodes of 20 minutes to 24 hours, fluctuating aural symptoms in the affected ear, and no better explanation. No documented hearing loss required.

He meets all four for definite. The audiogram does not have to be taken during an attack; the criterion says before, during or after, on at least one occasion, and today's is enough for the diagnosis. He has two, and the second shows the fluctuation objectively; that is more than the criteria ask for, and it is what good practice looks like. Serial audiograms are how you follow the disease from here: the drift toward a fixed loss, and the other ear. The fourth criterion is the one that asks you to think, and it is why the diagnosis waited until now: the mimics were closed by the questions in Step 4 and the tumor on the nerve by the MRI in Step 5. With those closed, the name is earned.

Why the others fail:
(B) The criterion accepts an audiogram before, during or after an episode. Between attacks counts, and he also has one from during an attack. Either alone would meet it.
(C) The criteria are clinical. Imaging is used to exclude the alternatives, which has been done, not to demonstrate hydrops; hydrops MRI exists as a research tool and is not part of the diagnosis.
(D) Electrocochleography is not part of the criteria and the guideline says not to use it to establish the diagnosis. It has a research role and is inconsistent in practice.

Keypoint: two attacks of 20 minutes to 12 hours, a documented low-frequency loss naming the ear, fluctuating aural symptoms, nothing else to explain it: definite.

Reference: Lopez-Escamez JA, Carey J, Chung WH, et al. Diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease. J Vestib Res. 2015;25(1):1-7. Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 1, 2 and 5.

steps.title: Step 7/7: What to Start
steps.scenario:
MRI normal.

    Attacks        2 or 3 a month
    Current drug   diphenidol every day, since the last emergency visit
    Why            he is afraid of the next attack

He asks whether there is anything better.
steps.question: What do you start, and what do you stop?

options.text: (A) Continue daily diphenidol and add a daily benzodiazepine
(B) A course of oral corticosteroid with each attack, as for sudden hearing loss

(C) Education and lifestyle: salt and caffeine restriction, sleep, stress; a trial of a diuretic or betahistine for prevention; a vestibular suppressant and antiemetic kept for attacks only, and the daily diphenidol stopped
(D) Intratympanic gentamicin now, to stop the attacks for good

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Meniere's disease is managed in tiers, and the first tier is not a drug.

Education. What the disease is, that it comes in attacks and remissions, that most people are controlled without invasive treatment, and that the hearing in the affected ear will probably decline over years regardless. The guideline lists this as a recommendation, not an option.

Lifestyle. Sodium restriction, less caffeine and alcohol, regular sleep, attention to stress. The evidence is weak but the cost is nothing, and some patients find their triggers.

Prevention, as an option. A diuretic such as hydrochlorothiazide, or betahistine. The evidence for both is thin and the guideline grades them as options, not recommendations. A trial for a few months is reasonable; if attacks do not fall, stop.

Rescue, for the attack itself. A vestibular suppressant such as diphenidol or a benzodiazepine, with an antiemetic, taken when an attack starts and stopped when it ends. This is the correction that matters most today: suppressants taken every day do not prevent attacks, they sedate him between them, and in a disease where the brain needs to compensate for a fluctuating ear they delay that compensation. The guideline says they are for acute attacks only.

Vestibular rehabilitation is for the chronic imbalance some patients develop between attacks, not for the attacks themselves.

If attacks continue despite all this, the next tier is intratympanic: corticosteroid first, because it costs the ear nothing; gentamicin, which ablates the ear's balance function and can cost hearing, only when the steroid has failed. That is a later visit.

Why the others fail:
(A) Daily suppressants sedate without preventing and hold back compensation. Adding a second one compounds it.
(B) Oral steroids are for a sudden sensorineural loss. Once the diagnosis is Meniere's disease, a steroid course with each of thirty attacks a year is harm without evidence.
(D) Gentamicin destroys the vestibular function of the ear and carries a real risk to its hearing. It is for attacks that have failed non-ablative treatment, not for a patient who has not yet had any.

Keypoint: educate, restrict salt and caffeine, try a diuretic or betahistine, keep the suppressant for attacks and stop it between them.

Reference: Basura GJ, Adams ME, Monfared A, et al. Clinical practice guideline: Meniere's disease. Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2020;162(2_suppl):S1-S55, Key Action Statements 7, 8 and 13.
